fig5_1: Four stacked one-dimensional node rows on a number line illustrate widening finite-difference stencils. In each row the central node x-i is marked red and the nodes contributing to its derivative are marked blue: a 3-point stencil (second order), then 5-point (fourth order), then 7-point (sixth order), and finally the spectral method, where every node on the line is highlighted. The takeaway is that a broader stencil raises accuracy, and the spectral case is the limit in which all nodes contribute, giving exponential rather than algebraic convergence.
fig5_2: Three side-by-side matrix sparsity patterns for twenty grid points, with nonzero entries shown as filled cells. Left: second-order finite differences form a narrow tridiagonal band of width three. Center: fourth-order finite differences form a pentadiagonal band of width five. Right: the spectral matrix is completely dense, with every off-diagonal entry filled. The sequence shows spectral methods as the limit of finite differences when the stencil spans the whole domain.
fig5_3: Overlaid curves of periodic cardinal functions phi-j on the interval zero to two pi for sixteen equispaced nodes. Each smooth oscillating curve rises to a value of one at its own node and crosses zero at every other node, satisfying the cardinal property. The oscillations damp smoothly with distance from each peak, with no growth toward the domain ends, unlike the boundary-amplified oscillations of Lagrange polynomials in non-periodic interpolation.
fig5_4: Two panels characterizing the periodic spectral differentiation matrix for sixteen points. Left: a color heatmap of the matrix entries showing constant-diagonal Toeplitz structure and skew-symmetry, with red positive values mirrored by blue negative values across the diagonal. Right: a scatter plot of the first-row entries D-zero-k against column offset k, with blue dots lying exactly on a dashed red curve given by one half times minus-one to the power k times cotangent of k pi over N, and an antisymmetric shape confirming the skew-symmetry.
fig5_5: Two panels showing spectral differentiation of u of x equals e to the power sine squared x with sixty-four points. Left: the navy function curve together with its first derivative, where the exact coral curve and the teal circle markers coincide. Right: the second derivative, with the exact purple curve and teal square markers coinciding. Maximum errors annotated in each panel are near machine precision, about ten to the power minus fourteen, demonstrating spectral accuracy for smooth periodic functions.
tbl5_1: Table reporting maximum errors in the first and second spectral derivatives of e to the power sine squared x as the grid size N grows from eight to sixty-four, showing both errors fall exponentially to machine precision by sixty-four points.
fig5_6: Triangular diagram of Fornberg's recursive algorithm drawn as a stencil pyramid. Each row is one level holding boxes that represent weights delta for node index k in a stencil of n plus one nodes, with the single-node top widening to the full stencil at the bottom. Green arrows show updates to existing node weights and red arrows show computation of each newly added node's weight, and the layered dependencies illustrate why the recursion is numerically stable.
fig5_7: Semilogarithmic plot of differentiation error versus grid size N, with error on a logarithmic vertical axis and N on a linear horizontal axis, for the test function one over two plus sine x. The three finite-difference curves, labelled FD2, FD4, and FD6, bend downward with progressively steeper algebraic slopes matching N to the minus two, minus four, and minus six, shown against dashed reference lines. The spectral curve falls as a straight line, reaching near machine precision around N equals fifty, dramatically outperforming the finite-difference schemes.
fig5_8: Four-panel grid showing the first four spectral derivatives of u of x equals e to the power minus sine of two x with thirty-two points. In each panel the exact derivative is a navy curve and the spectral approximation is overlaid colored markers that track it closely. Annotated maximum errors increase with derivative order, from about ten to the power minus seven for the first derivative up to about ten to the power minus two for the fourth, illustrating the intrinsic error amplification of repeated numerical differentiation.
tbl5_2: Table reporting maximum errors of the first through fourth spectral derivatives of e to the power minus sine of two x across grid sizes N from eight to sixty-four, showing exponential convergence for every order while higher derivatives need more points to reach a given accuracy.
fig5_9: Three panels on matrix squaring for second derivatives with sixteen points. Left: a heatmap of the squared matrix D-squared showing the same Toeplitz constant-diagonal pattern inherited from D. Center: a scatter comparing the eigenvalues of D-squared, drawn as circles, with the theoretical values minus k squared, drawn as squares, which coincide. Right: the second derivative of e to the power minus sine of two x computed by applying D-squared, with the numerical result matching the exact curve.
fig5_10: Two panels for the quantum harmonic oscillator solved by the periodic spectral method. Left: the first five eigenfunctions on the interval minus eight to eight using sixty-four points, with computed dots lying on the exact Hermite-function curves. Right: a semilog plot of eigenvalue error versus N for the first four eigenvalues, where each error curve drops faster than exponentially and reaches machine precision near N equals thirty-six.
tbl5_3: Table listing the harmonic oscillator eigenvalues computed by the periodic spectral method at N equals thirty-six, showing close agreement with the exact values lambda-n equals two n plus one.
